## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. While [unemployment in the district](https://www.statista.com/statistics/189405/unemployment-rate-in-district-of-columbia-since-1992/) has also been falling, it still had a [high poverty rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205446/poverty-rate-in-the-district-of-columbia/) in recent years.

## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. While [unemployment in the district](https://www.statista.com/statistics/189405/unemployment-rate-in-district-of-columbia-since-1992/) has also been falling, it still had a [high poverty rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205446/poverty-rate-in-the-district-of-columbia/) in recent years.

## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

# Violent crime in the United States - statistics & facts

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

In Minnesota, two recent ICE operations ended in fatal shootings, including the killing of [Renee Good](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659430/public-opinion-on-renee-good-ice-in-minneapolis-us/), thrusting the agency’s tactics and use of force into the national spotlight. The deaths came as [ICE detention was already surging](https://www.statista.com/chart/35665/number-of-ice-detainees/), with the number of people in custody reaching some of its highest levels by late 2025 as border encounters remained elevated. As the cases drew wider attention, public opinion hardened: [more Americans now support eliminating ICE altogether](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659429/public-opinion-on-abolishing-ice-in-the-us/), and [confidence in the agency’s ability to keep the country safe has eroded](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659431/public-opinion-on-ice-making-americans-safe-us/), especially because many respondents did not consider the shooting of Good justified. Together, these pressures have intensified a broader debate over whether aggressive immigration enforcement truly delivers security or instead fuels fear, mistrust, and enormous costs, with [large-scale deportation plans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659427/mass-deportation-immigrants-from-the-us-by-expense/) projected to require hundreds of billions of dollars, pushing questions about violent crime and state violence to the center of a national conversation.

## How are violent crimes defined?

Violent crime in the United States refers to offenses involving the use or threat of force, including murder and non-negligent manslaughter, rape and sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault. It is usually contrasted with property crime, which involves taking money or belongings without using force or threatening the victim; under this distinction, robbery counts as a violent crime, whereas burglary does not. Property crime still occurs far [more frequently than violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/), and aggravated assault makes up roughly two-thirds of all reported violent offenses. Over the past three decades, both the[total number and the rate of violent crime have dropped sharply](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191129/reported-violent-crime-in-the-us-since-1990/): reported incidents fell from about 1.93 million in 1992 to around 1.2 million in 2024, with the rate per 100,000 residents showing a similar long term decline once population growth is taken into account.

## Has violent crime truly gone down?

Despite the reported decline of violent crime, the U.S. still tops the global rankings for having [the most prisoners worldwide](https://www.statista.com/statistics/262961/countries-with-the-most-prisoners/) and the nation has had more [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/#topicOverview) and [school shootings](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1458029/number-of-shootings-in-public-and-private-schools-us/) than any other country, although they are generally not reported as a separate crime category owing to their relative infrequency. Violent crime figures may also be imprecise, as there is a[high rate of violent crimes not reported to police](https://www.statista.com/statistics/251934/usa-percentage-of-violent-crimes-reported-to-the-police/). This is particularly the case for rape and sexual assault, where only around one quarter of offenses are reported. In addition, national trends of crime are estimated by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), who rely on law enforcement agencies around the country to report their crime data accurately, which has not been the case in recent years. It is therefore almost certain that the actual rate of violent crime is considerably higher than official figures suggest. In this climate of disputed crime trends and rising anxiety about safety, recent incidents involving immigration authorities have become a key flashpoint in the broader debate over security, violent crime and state power, particularly [under Trump’s second administration](https://www.statista.com/study/175921/second-trump-administration/).

## Who are the victims of violence?

Studies have shown that violent crime victims belong to a diverse range of [age groups](https://www.statista.com/statistics/424130/us-violent-crime-victims-by-age/) and are almost equally divided by [gender](https://www.statista.com/statistics/423245/us-violent-crime-victims-by-gender/). These patterns indicate that risk is driven less by demographic labels alone and more by underlying conditions such as poverty, insecure work, and limited chances for social mobility. For instance, [38 percent of violent crime victims come from households earning under 25,000 U.S. dollars](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659485/violent-crime-victimiztion-rate-in-the-us-by-household-income/), compared with only 15.7 percent among households with incomes of 200,000 dollars or more.

# Violent crime in the United States - statistics & facts

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States

In Minnesota, two recent ICE operations ended in fatal shootings, including the killing of [Renee Good](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659430/public-opinion-on-renee-good-ice-in-minneapolis-us/), thrusting the agency’s tactics and use of force into the national spotlight. The deaths came as [ICE detention was already surging](https://www.statista.com/chart/35665/number-of-ice-detainees/), with the number of people in custody reaching some of its highest levels by late 2025 as border encounters remained elevated. As the cases drew wider attention, public opinion hardened: [more Americans now support eliminating ICE altogether](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659429/public-opinion-on-abolishing-ice-in-the-us/), and [confidence in the agency’s ability to keep the country safe has eroded](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659431/public-opinion-on-ice-making-americans-safe-us/), especially because many respondents did not consider the shooting of Good justified. Together, these pressures have intensified a broader debate over whether aggressive immigration enforcement truly delivers security or instead fuels fear, mistrust, and enormous costs, with [large-scale deportation plans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659427/mass-deportation-immigrants-from-the-us-by-expense/) projected to require hundreds of billions of dollars, pushing questions about violent crime and state violence to the center of a national conversation.

## How are violent crimes defined?

Violent crime in the United States refers to offenses involving the use or threat of force, including murder and non-negligent manslaughter, rape and sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault. It is usually contrasted with property crime, which involves taking money or belongings without using force or threatening the victim; under this distinction, robbery counts as a violent crime, whereas burglary does not. Property crime still occurs far [more frequently than violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/), and aggravated assault makes up roughly two-thirds of all reported violent offenses. Over the past three decades, both the[total number and the rate of violent crime have dropped sharply](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191129/reported-violent-crime-in-the-us-since-1990/): reported incidents fell from about 1.93 million in 1992 to around 1.2 million in 2024, with the rate per 100,000 residents showing a similar long term decline once population growth is taken into account.

## Has violent crime truly gone down?

Despite the reported decline of violent crime, the U.S. still tops the global rankings for having [the most prisoners worldwide](https://www.statista.com/statistics/262961/countries-with-the-most-prisoners/) and the nation has had more [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/#topicOverview) and [school shootings](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1458029/number-of-shootings-in-public-and-private-schools-us/) than any other country, although they are generally not reported as a separate crime category owing to their relative infrequency. Violent crime figures may also be imprecise, as there is a[high rate of violent crimes not reported to police](https://www.statista.com/statistics/251934/usa-percentage-of-violent-crimes-reported-to-the-police/). This is particularly the case for rape and sexual assault, where only around one quarter of offenses are reported. In addition, national trends of crime are estimated by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), who rely on law enforcement agencies around the country to report their crime data accurately, which has not been the case in recent years. It is therefore almost certain that the actual rate of violent crime is considerably higher than official figures suggest. In this climate of disputed crime trends and rising anxiety about safety, recent incidents involving immigration authorities have become a key flashpoint in the broader debate over security, violent crime and state power, particularly [under Trump’s second administration](https://www.statista.com/study/175921/second-trump-administration/).

## Who are the victims of violence?

Studies have shown that violent crime victims belong to a diverse range of [age groups](https://www.statista.com/statistics/424130/us-violent-crime-victims-by-age/) and are almost equally divided by [gender](https://www.statista.com/statistics/423245/us-violent-crime-victims-by-gender/). These patterns indicate that risk is driven less by demographic labels alone and more by underlying conditions such as poverty, insecure work, and limited chances for social mobility. For instance, [38 percent of violent crime victims come from households earning under 25,000 U.S. dollars](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659485/violent-crime-victimiztion-rate-in-the-us-by-household-income/), compared with only 15.7 percent among households with incomes of 200,000 dollars or more.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

Violent crime rate per 100k population by state (2023)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-FBI_2022-1)

This is a list of U.S. states and territories by violent crime rate. It is typically expressed in units of incidents per 100,000 individuals per year; thus, a violent crime rate of 300 (per 100,000 inhabitants) in a population of 100,000 would mean 300 incidents of violent crime per year in that entire population, or 0.3% out of the total. These data have been taken from the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI")'s [Uniform Crime Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Crime_Reports "Uniform Crime Reports").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-FBI_2022-1)

In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), violent crime consists of five types of criminal offenses: [murder and non-negligent manslaughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicide "Homicide"), [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape "Rape"), [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery "Robbery"), [aggravated assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aggravated_assault "Aggravated assault"), and [gang violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_violence "Gang violence").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-2)

Violent crime rate per 100k population by state (2023)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-FBI_2022-1)

This is a list of U.S. states and territories by violent crime rate. It is typically expressed in units of incidents per 100,000 individuals per year; thus, a violent crime rate of 300 (per 100,000 inhabitants) in a population of 100,000 would mean 300 incidents of violent crime per year in that entire population, or 0.3% out of the total. These data have been taken from the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI")'s [Uniform Crime Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Crime_Reports "Uniform Crime Reports").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-FBI_2022-1)

In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), violent crime consists of five types of criminal offenses: [murder and non-negligent manslaughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicide "Homicide"), [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape "Rape"), [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery "Robbery"), [aggravated assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aggravated_assault "Aggravated assault"), and [gang violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_violence "Gang violence").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_violent_crime_rate#cite_note-2)

# Which states have the highest and lowest crime rates?

Crime rates in the US hit record lows in 2024, while Hawaii saw the nation’s largest surge: violent crime was up 16.4%, and property crime was up 16.6%.

Updated Nov 26, 2025 by the[USAFacts team](https://usafacts.org/editorial-guidelines/)

In 2024, Alaska recorded the nation’s highest violent crime rate and New Mexico the highest property crime rate.

Maine had the lowest violent crime rate, and Idaho held the lowest property crime rate.

The US [crime rate](https://usafacts.org/answers/what-is-the-crime-rate-in-the-us/country/united-states/) has been trending downward for decades, including in 2024. While crime rates constantly fluctuate, overall violent crime and [property crime](https://usafacts.org/articles/property-crime-rates/) rates are both at their lowest points since 1976, the earliest year of available data.

State-by-state, though, crime rates vary because of factors like urbanization levels, economic conditions, and law enforcement effectiveness.

### What are violent and property crimes?

The Federal Bureau of Investigation's ([FBI](https://usafacts.org/explainers/what-does-the-us-government-do/subagency/federal-bureau-of-investigation/)) Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) [program](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/more-fbi-services-and-information/ucr) classifies violent crimes as those involving force or the threat of force. They are categorized into four specific offenses: murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault.

The UCR [defines](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/property-crime.pdf) property crime as a crime during which someone takes money or property without using force or threats. Property crimes includes burglary, larceny-theft, and motor vehicle theft.

Arson is also considered a property crime, and total offenses are reported, but the numbers are too small to calculate reliable rates—so the FBI does not publish arson rates.

### Get weekly insights

Subscribe for data-driven insights. No spin, just the facts.

## States with the highest and lowest crime rates

Alaska had the highest violent crime rate of any state in 2024, at 724.1 incidents per 100,000 residents, followed by New Mexico (717.1), Tennessee (592.3), Arkansas (579.4) and Louisiana (519.8).

The states with the least violent crimes were Maine (100.1), New Hampshire (110.1), Connecticut (136.0), Rhode Island (153.6), and Wyoming (203.4). The US average was 359.1 per 100,000 people.

## Alaska and New Mexico had the highest violent crime rates in 2024.

Reported violent crimes per 100,000 people by state, 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

New Mexico had the highest property crime rate among states that year, at 2,751.1 crimes per 100,000 residents, followed by Colorado (2,592.8), Washington state (2,466.5), Oregon (2,388.0), and Louisiana (2,296.4). The states with the fewest property crimes were Idaho (736.3), New Hampshire (918.0), Rhode Island (1,032.4), Massachusetts (1,112.1), and Maine (1,142.1). The US average was 1,760.1 per 100,000 people.

## New Mexico and Colorado had 2024’s highest property crime rates.

Reported property crimes per 100,000 people by state, 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

A range of factors influence variations in crime rates across states and regions. The [FBI identifies](https://ucr.fbi.gov/ucr-statistics-their-proper-use) elements that affect both the amount and type of crime, including:

*   Population density and urbanization 
*   Age — the youth population percentage 
*   Population stability, including mobility and commuting 
*   Transportation systems and infrastructure 
*   Economic factors like median income, poverty, and jobs 
*   Cultural, educational, and religious characteristics 
*   Family dynamics, including divorce rates and unity 
*   The climate 
*   Law enforcement strength 
*   Law enforcement strategies and focus 
*   Criminal justice system policies (prosecution, judiciary, corrections, probation) 
*   Public attitudes toward crime 
*   Crime reporting habits

## What are the crime rates in your area?

Reported violent and property crime rates by state, 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

Washington, DC, had higher crime rates in both categories than any state, but comparing its rates to other cities is more fitting. For more info on crime rates by city, read [Which cities have the highest or lowest crime rates?](https://usafacts.org/articles/how-does-crime-compare-by-city/)

## Which regions have the lowest and highest crime rates?

Northeastern states have the lowest crime rates among regions. Their violent crime rate was 22.1% lower than lower than the US average; the property crime rate was 16.9% lower.

In 2024, four of the five states with the lowest property crime rates and the four lowest violent crime rates were in the Northeast. New Hampshire, Maine, and Rhode Island were among the states with the lowest rates for both types.

Crime rates were highest in the West: the region’s violent crime rate was 21.0% higher than the rest of the country, and the property crime rate was 18.5% higher.

Western states had the four highest property crime rates and the two highest violent crime rates.

## How have crime rates changed over time?

The nation’s crime rate began consistently declining in the early 1990s. Since 1991 the national property crime rate has fallen every year except for one, and the violent crimes rate dropped in every year but five.

From 1976 to 2024, crime rates were lower for both property and violent crimes. Property crime went from a rate of 4,819.5 per 100,000 people in 1976 to 1,760.1, a decline of 63.5%. Violent crime dropped by 23.2% — from a rate of 467.8 per 100,000 in 1976 to 359.1 in 2024.

At the state level, property crime rates over the past 20 years are down in every state, and violent crime rates are down in 39 of 50.

## National crime rates have been generally declining since 1991.

Reported violent and property crime rates per 100,000 people, 1976–2024

Due to methodology disruptions, 2021 data is not comparable to other years. 

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

### Where have violent crime rates changed?

Violent crime rates decreased in 39 states and in Washington, DC, between 2004 and 2024. It declined by over 45% in Florida, Connecticut, and Illinois.

The three states with increases — North Dakota (221.3%), South Dakota (111.3%), and Vermont (95.6%) — had some of the nation’s lowest violent crime rates in 2004.

## Violent crime rates fell in 39 states and Washington, DC, since 2004.

Percent change in reported violent crime rates between 2004 and 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

Between 2023 and 2024, violent crime decreased in 36 states and in Washington, DC. The largest decreases were in Iowa (13.1%), Washington, DC (12.6%), and Alabama (10.9%), while the greatest annual increases were in Hawaii (16.4%), Wyoming (6.4%), and Vermont (4.1%)

Nationally, the violent crime rate fell 5.4% between 2023 and 2024 with the largest decline in the murder and nonnegligent manslaughter rate, which fell from 5.9 to 5.0, a 15.3% drop.

### Where have property crime rates changed?

The property crime rate in every state and Washington, DC, was lower in 2024 than in 2004. Property crime rates declined more than 65% in Idaho, Arizona, Florida, and Utah. North Dakota’s rate had the smallest decrease, at 12.2%.

## Property crime rates have fallen in every state and Washington, DC, since 2004.

Percent change in reported property crime rates between 2004 and 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

From 2023 to 2024, the property crime rate declined in 47 states and Washington, DC. Nebraska’s fell the most — 17.7% — followed by Wyoming (16.2%), Washington state (14.6%), and Washington, DC (14.3%). Of the three states with an increase, Hawaii’s rose the most: 16.6%.

Nationally, the property crime rate decreased by 9.0% between 2023 and 2024, with the largest decline being a 19.5% drop in motor vehicle thefts.

Larceny – the theft of personal property – made up 72.3% of property crimes included in FBI data, up from 60.6% of property crimes in 1976; the remaining crimes were motor vehicle theft (14.7%) and burglary (13.0%).

## Where does this data come from?

The FBI is the main government source of US crime data. Since 1929, it’s collected crime data from local law enforcement agencies through the Summary Reporting System (SRS). The FBI has used this data to estimate national, regional, and state crime statistics since the 1960s.

The FBI phased out the SRS in 2021 in favor of the more comprehensive [NIBRS](https://www.fbi.gov/services/cjis/ucr/nibrs), which collects data on single incidents instead of aggregated summaries of crimes, allowing the data to capture more specific crime information.

The latest data available from the SRS is from 2020, while the NIBRS has data through 2024.

Law enforcement agencies are still transitioning to the new system. As of 2024, agencies report to NIBRS covered 94.7% of the US population; in five states and Washington, DC, data covered 100% of the population.

## Mississippi and Florida had the lowest coverage of crime data reported to the FBI.

Percent of population served by NIBRS reporting agencies, 2024

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

The FBI has always used partial population data to estimate crime outcomes , even in areas that don’t report. The more agencies that report data to the FBI, the more accurate the estimates become. This article uses data from both the NIBRS and the SRS to shed light on both recent geographic trends and trends over time.

Note that the estimates used were calculated by the FBI using recent NIBRS data to replicate the estimation methodology previously applied to SRS data. This helps make the estimates comparable over time despite the change in reporting systems, although relatively lower reporting rates during the transition to NIBRS may still impact accuracy, so the data provided throughout this piece can still be used to approximate crime rate trends over time.

From 1976 to 2024, crime rates were lower for both property and violent crimes. Property crime went from a rate of 4,819.5 per 100,000 people in 1976 to 1,760.1, a decline of 63.5%. Violent crime dropped by 23.2% — from a rate of 467.8 per 100,000 in 1976 to 359.1 in 2024.

At the state level, property crime rates over the past 20 years are down in every state, and violent crime rates are down in 39 of 50.

## National crime rates have been generally declining since 1991.

Reported violent and property crime rates per 100,000 people, 1976–2024

Due to methodology disruptions, 2021 data is not comparable to other years. 

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

### Where have violent crime rates changed?

Violent crime rates decreased in 39 states and in Washington, DC, between 2004 and 2024. It declined by over 45% in Florida, Connecticut, and Illinois.

The three states with increases — North Dakota (221.3%), South Dakota (111.3%), and Vermont (95.6%) — had some of the nation’s lowest violent crime rates in 2004.

## Violent crime rates fell in 39 states and Washington, DC, since 2004.

Percent change in reported violent crime rates between 2004 and 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

Between 2023 and 2024, violent crime decreased in 36 states and in Washington, DC. The largest decreases were in Iowa (13.1%), Washington, DC (12.6%), and Alabama (10.9%), while the greatest annual increases were in Hawaii (16.4%), Wyoming (6.4%), and Vermont (4.1%)

Nationally, the violent crime rate fell 5.4% between 2023 and 2024 with the largest decline in the murder and nonnegligent manslaughter rate, which fell from 5.9 to 5.0, a 15.3% drop.

### Where have property crime rates changed?

The property crime rate in every state and Washington, DC, was lower in 2024 than in 2004. Property crime rates declined more than 65% in Idaho, Arizona, Florida, and Utah. North Dakota’s rate had the smallest decrease, at 12.2%.

## Property crime rates have fallen in every state and Washington, DC, since 2004.

Percent change in reported property crime rates between 2004 and 2024

Limited data for 2024 were available for Florida.

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

From 2023 to 2024, the property crime rate declined in 47 states and Washington, DC. Nebraska’s fell the most — 17.7% — followed by Wyoming (16.2%), Washington state (14.6%), and Washington, DC (14.3%). Of the three states with an increase, Hawaii’s rose the most: 16.6%.

Nationally, the property crime rate decreased by 9.0% between 2023 and 2024, with the largest decline being a 19.5% drop in motor vehicle thefts.

Larceny – the theft of personal property – made up 72.3% of property crimes included in FBI data, up from 60.6% of property crimes in 1976; the remaining crimes were motor vehicle theft (14.7%) and burglary (13.0%).

## Where does this data come from?

The FBI is the main government source of US crime data. Since 1929, it’s collected crime data from local law enforcement agencies through the Summary Reporting System (SRS). The FBI has used this data to estimate national, regional, and state crime statistics since the 1960s.

The FBI phased out the SRS in 2021 in favor of the more comprehensive [NIBRS](https://www.fbi.gov/services/cjis/ucr/nibrs), which collects data on single incidents instead of aggregated summaries of crimes, allowing the data to capture more specific crime information.

The latest data available from the SRS is from 2020, while the NIBRS has data through 2024.

Law enforcement agencies are still transitioning to the new system. As of 2024, agencies report to NIBRS covered 94.7% of the US population; in five states and Washington, DC, data covered 100% of the population.

## Mississippi and Florida had the lowest coverage of crime data reported to the FBI.

Percent of population served by NIBRS reporting agencies, 2024

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

The FBI has always used partial population data to estimate crime outcomes , even in areas that don’t report. The more agencies that report data to the FBI, the more accurate the estimates become. This article uses data from both the NIBRS and the SRS to shed light on both recent geographic trends and trends over time.

Note that the estimates used were calculated by the FBI using recent NIBRS data to replicate the estimation methodology previously applied to SRS data. This helps make the estimates comparable over time despite the change in reporting systems, although relatively lower reporting rates during the transition to NIBRS may still impact accuracy, so the data provided throughout this piece can still be used to approximate crime rate trends over time.

## Sources

The [CDC WONDER](https://wonder.cdc.gov/) Online Database is the source of the 2024 [National Vital Statistics System](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/index.htm) death data featured in Stats of the States.

Where states are ranked, states are categorized from highest rate to lowest rate. Mortality rankings and rates are based on 2024 age-adjusted death rates.

**Keep Reading**[Age Standardization of Death Rates: Implementation of the Year 2000 Standard](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr47/nvs47_03.pdf)

Although adjusted for variations in age distribution and population size, differences by state do not account for other state-specific population characteristics that may affect death rates.

When the number of deaths is small, differences between states and rankings by state may be unreliable due to instability in rates. The map and table will not show death rates that do not meet [National Center for Health Statistics](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/index.html) standards for data reliability.

**Keep Reading**[National Center for Health Statistics Data Presentation Standards for Rates and Counts](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/series/sr_02/sr02-200.pdf)

The [CDC WONDER](https://wonder.cdc.gov/) Online Database is the source of the 2024 [National Vital Statistics System](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/index.htm) death data featured in Stats of the States.

Where states are ranked, states are categorized from highest rate to lowest rate. Mortality rankings and rates are based on 2024 age-adjusted death rates.

**Keep Reading**[Age Standardization of Death Rates: Implementation of the Year 2000 Standard](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr47/nvs47_03.pdf)

Although adjusted for variations in age distribution and population size, differences by state do not account for other state-specific population characteristics that may affect death rates.

When the number of deaths is small, differences between states and rankings by state may be unreliable due to instability in rates. The map and table will not show death rates that do not meet [National Center for Health Statistics](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/index.html) standards for data reliability.

# Property crime in the United States - statistics & facts

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

 Property crime in the United States incorporates all instances of theft or unlawful destruction of property in the absence of force or threat of force against a victim. As with the [rate of violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/), the [property crime rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) in the United States has dropped dramatically since 1990. Of the different forms of property crime, [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) is the most common in the U.S. with over [4.51 million](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191211/reported-larceny-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) reported cases in 2023. Among such cases, [theft of items from motor vehicles](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195203/larceny-theft-in-the-us-by-type/) is the most common type. Interestingly, survey data shows that although crime rates have continued to drop, a [majority of Americans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) have persistently believed that there was more crime in the current year than the year before. This may also reflect the fact that national crime trends are reported by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), whose data is based solely off information received from participating law enforcement agencies around the country. However, not all agencies [participate every year](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/), making it difficult to say for sure how much property crime is actually occurring nationwide. 

  

## Property crime and financial gain

 New Mexico is a hot bed for property crime. The state has the highest [burglary rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232580/burglary-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), one of the highest [larceny-theft rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232583/larceny-theft-rate-in-the-us-by-state/) and one of the highest [motor vehicle theft rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232588/motor-vehicle-theft-rate-in-the-us-by-state/) in the country. In contrast to arson and many violent crimes, people generally seek to commit theft related property crimes because of the expected personal financial gain from committing such crimes. As such, it can be expected that the crime rates will be higher in areas where poverty rates are higher than national averages. The immorality of theft subsides to a perceived necessity for those facing a dire financial situation. Unsurprisingly, [New Mexico has the second highest poverty rate in the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/233093/us-poverty-rate-by-state/) as of 2023.   
  

## Clearance rates

 Another potential reason people may choose to commit property crimes is the likelihood of them being caught and therefore charged. A look at the [crime clearance rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/194213/crime-clearance-rate-by-type-in-the-us/) for different crimes in the United States shows that people are much less likely to be caught when committing property crimes than violent crimes. The crime criminals appear most likely to get away with the most in the United States is motor vehicle theft. Additionally, only 26.2 percent of arsons are cleared through arrest or other exceptional means. Among crimes of arson, it is even more unlikely that someone will be caught for [arson of a motor vehicle](https://www.statista.com/statistics/252463/clearance-rate-of-arson-offenses-in-the-united-states-by-type/).

# Property crime in the United States - statistics & facts

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

 Property crime in the United States incorporates all instances of theft or unlawful destruction of property in the absence of force or threat of force against a victim. As with the [rate of violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/), the [property crime rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) in the United States has dropped dramatically since 1990. Of the different forms of property crime, [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) is the most common in the U.S. with over [4.51 million](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191211/reported-larceny-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) reported cases in 2023. Among such cases, [theft of items from motor vehicles](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195203/larceny-theft-in-the-us-by-type/) is the most common type. Interestingly, survey data shows that although crime rates have continued to drop, a [majority of Americans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) have persistently believed that there was more crime in the current year than the year before. This may also reflect the fact that national crime trends are reported by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), whose data is based solely off information received from participating law enforcement agencies around the country. However, not all agencies [participate every year](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/), making it difficult to say for sure how much property crime is actually occurring nationwide. 

  

## Property crime and financial gain

 New Mexico is a hot bed for property crime. The state has the highest [burglary rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232580/burglary-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), one of the highest [larceny-theft rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232583/larceny-theft-rate-in-the-us-by-state/) and one of the highest [motor vehicle theft rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232588/motor-vehicle-theft-rate-in-the-us-by-state/) in the country. In contrast to arson and many violent crimes, people generally seek to commit theft related property crimes because of the expected personal financial gain from committing such crimes. As such, it can be expected that the crime rates will be higher in areas where poverty rates are higher than national averages. The immorality of theft subsides to a perceived necessity for those facing a dire financial situation. Unsurprisingly, [New Mexico has the second highest poverty rate in the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/233093/us-poverty-rate-by-state/) as of 2023.   
  

## Clearance rates

 Another potential reason people may choose to commit property crimes is the likelihood of them being caught and therefore charged. A look at the [crime clearance rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/194213/crime-clearance-rate-by-type-in-the-us/) for different crimes in the United States shows that people are much less likely to be caught when committing property crimes than violent crimes. The crime criminals appear most likely to get away with the most in the United States is motor vehicle theft. Additionally, only 26.2 percent of arsons are cleared through arrest or other exceptional means. Among crimes of arson, it is even more unlikely that someone will be caught for [arson of a motor vehicle](https://www.statista.com/statistics/252463/clearance-rate-of-arson-offenses-in-the-united-states-by-type/).

# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. While [unemployment in the district](https://www.statista.com/statistics/189405/unemployment-rate-in-district-of-columbia-since-1992/) has also been falling, it still had a [high poverty rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205446/poverty-rate-in-the-district-of-columbia/) in recent years.

## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. ## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

# Violent Crime Stable, Property Crime Rebounds

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Nov 17, 2023 

 Crime in the United States 

Larceny-theft and burglary have become less widespread [in the U.S.](https://www.statista.com/topics/2153/crime-in-the-united-states/) since 2012. In the pandemic, this decrease sped up - before a resurgence in the theft category happened in 2022. Despite property crime levels remaining below those of 2019, the yearlong downward trend in the category nevertheless seems broken.

Motor vehicle theft, meanwhile, decoupled from the greater larceny-theft trend and has skyrocketed throughout the pandemic. It is, however, a less common type of crime in the country. [Violent crime](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/), including homicide, rape, robbery and aggravated assault, remained mostly stable since 2012. A large spike in murders did happen in the pandemic, but since the crime makes up just a small part of the violent crime category, these changes are not visible in overall numbers.

News of organized retail theft, sometimes called smash and grab incidents, have continued to be reported from different parts of the country, receiving much attention from the public [as well as from policymakers](https://apnews.com/article/california-smash-grab-robberies-grants-police-0172b4e64ed9d748a6fced4316f4121d/). At least until 2021, the share of shoplifting incidents involving more than two people remained at less than 5 percent, while crimes with more than six participants made up just 0.1 percent of the total, according to [data analyzed by the Council on Criminal Justice.](https://counciloncj.org/shoplifting-trends-what-you-need-to-know/)

The same organization found a mixed picture when looking at retail theft [in a sample of 24 U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/chart/31272/number-of-shoplifting-incidents-per-100000-people-in-selected-us-cities/), concluding that shoplifting in particular saw a major dip in the pandemic and a resurgence after. Most cities, however, also remain below pre-pandemic levels, with some notable exceptions. New York City saw a large increase in retail theft in 2023, while 2019 and 2018 rates were also surpassed in Boston and Los Angeles.

# Violent Crime Stable, Property Crime Rebounds

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Nov 17, 2023 

 Crime in the United States 

Larceny-theft and burglary have become less widespread [in the U.S.](https://www.statista.com/topics/2153/crime-in-the-united-states/) since 2012. In the pandemic, this decrease sped up - before a resurgence in the theft category happened in 2022. Despite property crime levels remaining below those of 2019, the yearlong downward trend in the category nevertheless seems broken.

Motor vehicle theft, meanwhile, decoupled from the greater larceny-theft trend and has skyrocketed throughout the pandemic. It is, however, a less common type of crime in the country. [Violent crime](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/), including homicide, rape, robbery and aggravated assault, remained mostly stable since 2012. A large spike in murders did happen in the pandemic, but since the crime makes up just a small part of the violent crime category, these changes are not visible in overall numbers.

News of organized retail theft, sometimes called smash and grab incidents, have continued to be reported from different parts of the country, receiving much attention from the public [as well as from policymakers](https://apnews.com/article/california-smash-grab-robberies-grants-police-0172b4e64ed9d748a6fced4316f4121d/). At least until 2021, the share of shoplifting incidents involving more than two people remained at less than 5 percent, while crimes with more than six participants made up just 0.1 percent of the total, according to [data analyzed by the Council on Criminal Justice.](https://counciloncj.org/shoplifting-trends-what-you-need-to-know/)

The same organization found a mixed picture when looking at retail theft [in a sample of 24 U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/chart/31272/number-of-shoplifting-incidents-per-100000-people-in-selected-us-cities/), concluding that shoplifting in particular saw a major dip in the pandemic and a resurgence after. Most cities, however, also remain below pre-pandemic levels, with some notable exceptions. New York City saw a large increase in retail theft in 2023, while 2019 and 2018 rates were also surpassed in Boston and Los Angeles.

In 2024, an estimated 1,221,345 violent crimes occurred in the United States. This was a decrease from the previous year, when 1,278,301 violent crimes were reported.

## Violent crime in the United States

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reported that violent crime was at a high of 1.93 million crimes in 1992 and fell to a low of 1.15 million violent crimes in 2014. When conducting crime reporting, the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program considered murder, nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault to be violent crimes, because they are offenses that involve force or threat of violence.

## California, Texas, Florida top the list

In 2024, California ranked first [among U.S. states by number of murders](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195331/number-of-murders-in-the-us-by-state/), followed by Texas, and Florida. The greatest number of murders were committed by perpetrators with an 'unknown' relationship to their victim. 'Girlfriend' was the fourth most common relationship of victim to offender, with a reported 568 partners murdering their girlfriends that year.

In 2024, an estimated 1,221,345 violent crimes occurred in the United States. This was a decrease from the previous year, when 1,278,301 violent crimes were reported.

## Violent crime in the United States

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reported that violent crime was at a high of 1.93 million crimes in 1992 and fell to a low of 1.15 million violent crimes in 2014. When conducting crime reporting, the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program considered murder, nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault to be violent crimes, because they are offenses that involve force or threat of violence.

## California, Texas, Florida top the list

In 2024, California ranked first [among U.S. states by number of murders](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195331/number-of-murders-in-the-us-by-state/), followed by Texas, and Florida. The greatest number of murders were committed by perpetrators with an 'unknown' relationship to their victim. 'Girlfriend' was the fourth most common relationship of victim to offender, with a reported 568 partners murdering their girlfriends that year.

## Crime rate

The crime rate in the United States has generally decreased over time. There are several factors attributed to the [decrease in the crime rate across the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/301560/us-crimes-committed-state/). An increase in the number of police officers and an increase in income are some of the reasons for a decrease in the crime rate. Unfortunately, people of color have been disproportionately affected by crime rates, as they are more likely to be arrested for a crime versus a white person.

## Crime rates regionally

The District of Columbia had the [highest rate of reported violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) in the United States in 2023 per 100,000 inhabitants. The most common [crime clearance type in metropolitan counties in the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/194206/crime-clearance-rate-in-metropolitan-counties-by-type-in-the-us/) in 2020 was murder and non-negligent manslaughter. The [second most dangerous city in the country](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/) in 2020 was Detroit. Detroit has faced severe levels of economic and demographic declines in the past years. Not only has the population decreased, the city has filed for bankruptcy. Despite the median household income increasing, the city still struggles financially.

## Crime rate

The crime rate in the United States has generally decreased over time. There are several factors attributed to the [decrease in the crime rate across the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/301560/us-crimes-committed-state/). An increase in the number of police officers and an increase in income are some of the reasons for a decrease in the crime rate. Unfortunately, people of color have been disproportionately affected by crime rates, as they are more likely to be arrested for a crime versus a white person.

## Crime rates regionally

The District of Columbia had the [highest rate of reported violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) in the United States in 2023 per 100,000 inhabitants. The most common [crime clearance type in metropolitan counties in the United States](https://www.statista.com/statistics/194206/crime-clearance-rate-in-metropolitan-counties-by-type-in-the-us/) in 2020 was murder and non-negligent manslaughter. The [second most dangerous city in the country](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/) in 2020 was Detroit. Detroit has faced severe levels of economic and demographic declines in the past years. Not only has the population decreased, the city has filed for bankruptcy. Despite the median household income increasing, the city still struggles financially.

In 2024, an estimated 1,221,345 violent crimes occurred in the United States. This was a decrease from the previous year, when 1,278,301 violent crimes were reported.

## Violent crime in the United States

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reported that violent crime was at a high of 1.93 million crimes in 1992 and fell to a low of 1.15 million violent crimes in 2014. When conducting crime reporting, the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program considered murder, nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault to be violent crimes, because they are offenses that involve force or threat of violence.

## California, Texas, Florida top the list

In 2024, California ranked first [among U.S. states by number of murders](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195331/number-of-murders-in-the-us-by-state/), followed by Texas, and Florida. The greatest number of murders were committed by perpetrators with an 'unknown' relationship to their victim. 'Girlfriend' was the fourth most common relationship of victim to offender, with a reported 568 partners murdering their girlfriends that year.

In 2024, an estimated 1,221,345 violent crimes occurred in the United States. This was a decrease from the previous year, when 1,278,301 violent crimes were reported.

## Violent crime in the United States

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reported that violent crime was at a high of 1.93 million crimes in 1992 and fell to a low of 1.15 million violent crimes in 2014. When conducting crime reporting, the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting Program considered murder, nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault to be violent crimes, because they are offenses that involve force or threat of violence.

## California, Texas, Florida top the list

In 2024, California ranked first [among U.S. states by number of murders](https://www.statista.com/statistics/195331/number-of-murders-in-the-us-by-state/), followed by Texas, and Florida. The greatest number of murders were committed by perpetrators with an 'unknown' relationship to their victim. 'Girlfriend' was the fourth most common relationship of victim to offender, with a reported 568 partners murdering their girlfriends that year.
