# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

# Crime in the United states

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

The topic of crime in the United States is broad, technically covering any action punishable under state or federal law. One common way to narrow the scope is to focus on offenses involving jail time and then differentiate between [violent crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) and [property crimes](https://www.statista.com/topics/1751/property-crime-in-the-us/). Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force against a person, while property crimes involve the taking of money or goods without direct confrontation. Property crimes significantly outnumber violent crimes, with [larceny-theft](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/) remaining the most commonly committed offense by a wide margin.

## Crime rates continued to fall in 2024

According to the FBI's latest data, both [violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191219/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-usa-since-1990/) and [property crime rates](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191237/reported-property-crime-rate-in-the-us-since-1990/) dropped significantly in 2024, reaching their lowest levels in roughly two decades. The decline was broad-based: [murder and nonnegligent manslaughter](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191134/reported-murder-and-nonnegligent-manslaughter-cases-in-the-us-since-1990/) cases saw particularly sharp decreases, while robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, and motor vehicle theft all trended downward as well. Researchers largely attribute the continued drop to the unwinding of pandemic-era stressors that had fueled a surge in homicides between 2020 and 2022. Despite the national downward trend, significant geographic variation remains. States such as New Mexico, Louisiana, and Colorado continued to report high rates of both [violent](https://www.statista.com/statistics/200445/reported-violent-crime-rate-in-the-us-states/) and [property crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/232575/property-crime-rate-in-the-us-by-state/), while New England states generally recorded some of the lowest rates. Washington, D.C. technically topped several crime rate lists, though this result is misleading due to its strictly urban geography; when compared to [other major U.S. cities](https://www.statista.com/statistics/217685/most-dangerous-cities-in-north-america-by-crime-rate/), the capital ranked behind multiple metropolitan areas.

## Public perception does not match the data

Despite sustained decreases, surveys consistently show that a majority of Americans believe [crime is increasing](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205525/public-perception-of-trend-in-crime-problem-in-the-usa/) each year. This gap between perception and reality has persisted for decades and is partly fueled by extensive media coverage of high-profile incidents. Critics point out that while the FBI's overall figures have improved, areas such as [gun violence](https://www.statista.com/topics/10904/gun-violence-in-the-united-states/) and [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/) continue to shape public anxiety and dominate the national conversation around safety. Additionally, the FBI's transition to its new National Incident-Based Reporting System has improved data quality, but gaps in [agency reporting](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1368634/crime-data-reported-fbi-by-state-us/) mean national crime figures may still undercount the true scope of criminal activity across the country.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

# Violent Crime Rates Fall in the U.S.

by[Katharina Buchholz](mailto:katharina.buchholz@statista.com), 

 Oct 18, 2023 

 Violent crime in the United States 

[The violent crime rate](https://www.statista.com/topics/1750/violent-crime-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, [an annual release from the FBI has found.](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/explorer/crime/crime-trend) There were 380.7 violent crimes per 100,000 people reported to the FBI from law enforcement agencies last year, a 0.1 point decrease from 2019. In 2020, the rate had been as high as 398.5, while the FBI estimates that it stood at 387.0 in 2021.

2020 saw a spike in murders and aggrevated assaults in the U.S. that has not been fully understood. Reasons like pandemic stress, the proliferation of [guns](https://www.statista.com/topics/1287/firearms-in-the-us/) in the country and distrust in police have been named as potential reasons. Rates for both crime types have come down in 2022 but remain above pre-pandemic levels. It is due to the decrease in the rate of rapes and robberies, which are lower now than before the pandemic, that the overall rate of violent crime has come down to 2019 levels once again.

Looking at property crimes, including motor vehicle theft, burglary, larceny and theft, the rate stood at 1,954.4 incidents in 2022, up from 1,832.3 in 2021. It was the first rise in many years as the rate had been falling almost continuously since the 1990s. While burglary rates continued to drop, motor vehicle theft as well as the more common larceny-theft category have been seeing rising rates since 2020 and 2021, respectively.

In the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program, violent crime is composed of four offenses: murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. Violent crimes are defined in the UCR Program as those offenses that involve force or threat of force.  
  
Due to the FBI's transition to a new crime reporting system, not all law enforcement agencies submitted crime data to the FBI. As a result, figures may not accurately reflect the total number of crimes and are not comparable to previous years' data.

## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. While [unemployment in the district](https://www.statista.com/statistics/189405/unemployment-rate-in-district-of-columbia-since-1992/) has also been falling, it still had a [high poverty rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205446/poverty-rate-in-the-district-of-columbia/) in recent years.

## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

 Supplementary notes 

In the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program, violent crime is composed of four offenses: murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, forcible rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. Violent crimes are defined in the UCR Program as those offenses that involve force or threat of force.  
  
Due to the FBI's transition to a new crime reporting system, not all law enforcement agencies submitted crime data to the FBI. As a result, figures may not accurately reflect the total number of crimes and are not comparable to previous years' data.

## Life in the District

The District of Columbia has seen [fluctuating population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/206105/resident-population-in-district-of-columbia/) growth over the past few decades. Its population declined throughout the 1990s, when crime rates were at their peak, but has recovered since then. While [unemployment in the district](https://www.statista.com/statistics/189405/unemployment-rate-in-district-of-columbia-since-1992/) has also been falling, it still had a [high poverty rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/205446/poverty-rate-in-the-district-of-columbia/) in recent years.

## Law enforcement in the U.S.

Crime rates in the U.S. have decreased compared to previous years, although many Americans still perceive crime as an important issue. The [number of law enforcement officers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191694/number-of-law-enforcement-officers-in-the-us/) in the U.S. has recently increased. Additionally, initiatives by the Justice Department, focused on community-based prevention and intervention programs, have further helped lower violent crime rates.

# What is the crime rate in the US?

Updated Jun. 5, 2026 Refreshed annually

In 2024, for every 100,000 people, the violent crime rate was 359 and the property crime rate was 1,760. Simply speaking, violent crimes are committed against people, property crimes are not. These crime rates do not include every violent and property crime, but rather four violent offenses and three property offenses that have been tracked since 1929.

The combined violent and property crime rate in the US fell 8.4% versus the previous year, driven by a 5.4% decrease in the violent crime rate and a 9% decrease in the property crime rate. Since 2001, that overall crime rate is down 49.1%.

Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force, and include:   

*   Murder and non-negligent manslaughter
*   Rape

In 2024, the highest and lowest violent crime rates among states were in Alaska at 724 offenses per 100,000 people and Maine at 100. The highest property crime rate was in New Mexico at 2,751 per 100,000 while the lowest was in Idaho at 736.

# What is the crime rate in the US?

Updated Jun. 5, 2026 Refreshed annually

In 2024, for every 100,000 people, the violent crime rate was 359 and the property crime rate was 1,760. Simply speaking, violent crimes are committed against people, property crimes are not. These crime rates do not include every violent and property crime, but rather four violent offenses and three property offenses that have been tracked since 1929.

359

violent crimes per 100K people (2024)

1,760

property crimes per 100K people (2024)

Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation

The combined violent and property crime rate in the US fell 8.4% versus the previous year, driven by a 5.4% decrease in the violent crime rate and a 9% decrease in the property crime rate. Since 2001, that overall crime rate is down 49.1%.

## What is violent crime? Has it increased or decreased over time?

Violent crimes involve force or the threat of force, and include:   

*   Murder and non-negligent manslaughter
*   Rape
*   Robbery (the [FBI defines this](https://le.fbi.gov/file-repository/nibrs-user-manual-2025-0-062625.pdf/view) as “... taking or attempting to take something of value from a victim ... by the use of force or threat of force ...”; the victim must be present).
*   Aggravated assault

In 2024, there was about one violent offense for every 278 people. 71.3% of all violent crimes were aggravated assaults; 16.9%, robberies; 10.4%, rapes; and 1.4%, murders.

## What is property crime? Has it increased or decreased over time?

Property crimes involve the taking of money or property without force or the threat of it, and include:   

*   Burglary (the [FBI defines this](https://le.fbi.gov/file-repository/nibrs-user-manual-2025-0-062625.pdf/view) as “the unlawful entry into a building or some other structure to commit a felony or a theft”).
*   Larceny-theft, often called stealing (the [FBI defines this](https://le.fbi.gov/file-repository/nibrs-user-manual-2025-0-062625.pdf/view) as “the unlawful taking, carrying, leading, or riding away of property from the possession or constructive possession of another person”).
*   Motor vehicle theft (not included in larceny-theft)

In 2024, there was about one property [crime](https://usafacts.org/crime/) for every 57 people. 72.3% of all property crimes were larceny-thefts; 14.7%, motor vehicle thefts; and 13%, burglaries.

## What state has the highest crime rate? What state has the lowest?

In 2024, the highest and lowest violent crime rates among states were in Alaska at 724 offenses per 100,000 people and Maine at 100. The highest property crime rate was in New Mexico at 2,751 per 100,000 while the lowest was in Idaho at 736.

Washington, DC is also factored into the country’s overall crime rate. It had a violent crime rate of 1,006 offenses per 100,000 and a property crime rate of 3,693.

# Violent crime in the United States - statistics & facts

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States 

*   Overview
*   Editor’s Picks
*   Statistics

In Minnesota, two recent ICE operations ended in fatal shootings, including the killing of [Renee Good](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659430/public-opinion-on-renee-good-ice-in-minneapolis-us/), thrusting the agency’s tactics and use of force into the national spotlight. The deaths came as [ICE detention was already surging](https://www.statista.com/chart/35665/number-of-ice-detainees/), with the number of people in custody reaching some of its highest levels by late 2025 as border encounters remained elevated. As the cases drew wider attention, public opinion hardened: [more Americans now support eliminating ICE altogether](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659429/public-opinion-on-abolishing-ice-in-the-us/), and [confidence in the agency’s ability to keep the country safe has eroded](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659431/public-opinion-on-ice-making-americans-safe-us/), especially because many respondents did not consider the shooting of Good justified. Together, these pressures have intensified a broader debate over whether aggressive immigration enforcement truly delivers security or instead fuels fear, mistrust, and enormous costs, with [large-scale deportation plans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659427/mass-deportation-immigrants-from-the-us-by-expense/) projected to require hundreds of billions of dollars, pushing questions about violent crime and state violence to the center of a national conversation.

## How are violent crimes defined?

Violent crime in the United States refers to offenses involving the use or threat of force, including murder and non-negligent manslaughter, rape and sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault. It is usually contrasted with property crime, which involves taking money or belongings without using force or threatening the victim; under this distinction, robbery counts as a violent crime, whereas burglary does not. Property crime still occurs far [more frequently than violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/), and aggravated assault makes up roughly two-thirds of all reported violent offenses. Over the past three decades, both the[total number and the rate of violent crime have dropped sharply](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191129/reported-violent-crime-in-the-us-since-1990/): reported incidents fell from about 1.93 million in 1992 to around 1.2 million in 2024, with the rate per 100,000 residents showing a similar long term decline once population growth is taken into account.

## Has violent crime truly gone down?

Despite the reported decline of violent crime, the U.S. still tops the global rankings for having [the most prisoners worldwide](https://www.statista.com/statistics/262961/countries-with-the-most-prisoners/) and the nation has had more [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/#topicOverview) and [school shootings](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1458029/number-of-shootings-in-public-and-private-schools-us/) than any other country, although they are generally not reported as a separate crime category owing to their relative infrequency. Violent crime figures may also be imprecise, as there is a[high rate of violent crimes not reported to police](https://www.statista.com/statistics/251934/usa-percentage-of-violent-crimes-reported-to-the-police/). This is particularly the case for rape and sexual assault, where only around one quarter of offenses are reported. In addition, national trends of crime are estimated by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), who rely on law enforcement agencies around the country to report their crime data accurately, which has not been the case in recent years. It is therefore almost certain that the actual rate of violent crime is considerably higher than official figures suggest. In this climate of disputed crime trends and rising anxiety about safety, recent incidents involving immigration authorities have become a key flashpoint in the broader debate over security, violent crime and state power, particularly [under Trump’s second administration](https://www.statista.com/study/175921/second-trump-administration/).

## Who are the victims of violence?

Studies have shown that violent crime victims belong to a diverse range of [age groups](https://www.statista.com/statistics/424130/us-violent-crime-victims-by-age/) and are almost equally divided by [gender](https://www.statista.com/statistics/423245/us-violent-crime-victims-by-gender/). These patterns indicate that risk is driven less by demographic labels alone and more by underlying conditions such as poverty, insecure work, and limited chances for social mobility. For instance, [38 percent of violent crime victims come from households earning under 25,000 U.S. dollars](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659485/violent-crime-victimiztion-rate-in-the-us-by-household-income/), compared with only 15.7 percent among households with incomes of 200,000 dollars or more.

# Violent crime in the United States - statistics & facts

 Region  United States  United States 

 Choose a region: ![Image 1: United States](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/US.svg) United States

In Minnesota, two recent ICE operations ended in fatal shootings, including the killing of [Renee Good](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659430/public-opinion-on-renee-good-ice-in-minneapolis-us/), thrusting the agency’s tactics and use of force into the national spotlight. The deaths came as [ICE detention was already surging](https://www.statista.com/chart/35665/number-of-ice-detainees/), with the number of people in custody reaching some of its highest levels by late 2025 as border encounters remained elevated. As the cases drew wider attention, public opinion hardened: [more Americans now support eliminating ICE altogether](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659429/public-opinion-on-abolishing-ice-in-the-us/), and [confidence in the agency’s ability to keep the country safe has eroded](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659431/public-opinion-on-ice-making-americans-safe-us/), especially because many respondents did not consider the shooting of Good justified. Together, these pressures have intensified a broader debate over whether aggressive immigration enforcement truly delivers security or instead fuels fear, mistrust, and enormous costs, with [large-scale deportation plans](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659427/mass-deportation-immigrants-from-the-us-by-expense/) projected to require hundreds of billions of dollars, pushing questions about violent crime and state violence to the center of a national conversation.

## How are violent crimes defined?

Violent crime in the United States refers to offenses involving the use or threat of force, including murder and non-negligent manslaughter, rape and sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault. It is usually contrasted with property crime, which involves taking money or belongings without using force or threatening the victim; under this distinction, robbery counts as a violent crime, whereas burglary does not. Property crime still occurs far [more frequently than violent crime](https://www.statista.com/statistics/202714/number-of-committed-crimes-in-the-us-by-type-of-crime/), and aggravated assault makes up roughly two-thirds of all reported violent offenses. Over the past three decades, both the[total number and the rate of violent crime have dropped sharply](https://www.statista.com/statistics/191129/reported-violent-crime-in-the-us-since-1990/): reported incidents fell from about 1.93 million in 1992 to around 1.2 million in 2024, with the rate per 100,000 residents showing a similar long term decline once population growth is taken into account.

## Has violent crime truly gone down?

Despite the reported decline of violent crime, the U.S. still tops the global rankings for having [the most prisoners worldwide](https://www.statista.com/statistics/262961/countries-with-the-most-prisoners/) and the nation has had more [mass shootings](https://www.statista.com/topics/10843/mass-shootings-in-the-united-states/#topicOverview) and [school shootings](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1458029/number-of-shootings-in-public-and-private-schools-us/) than any other country, although they are generally not reported as a separate crime category owing to their relative infrequency. Violent crime figures may also be imprecise, as there is a[high rate of violent crimes not reported to police](https://www.statista.com/statistics/251934/usa-percentage-of-violent-crimes-reported-to-the-police/). This is particularly the case for rape and sexual assault, where only around one quarter of offenses are reported. In addition, national trends of crime are estimated by the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://www.statista.com/topics/10632/the-fbi/#topicOverview), who rely on law enforcement agencies around the country to report their crime data accurately, which has not been the case in recent years. It is therefore almost certain that the actual rate of violent crime is considerably higher than official figures suggest. In this climate of disputed crime trends and rising anxiety about safety, recent incidents involving immigration authorities have become a key flashpoint in the broader debate over security, violent crime and state power, particularly [under Trump’s second administration](https://www.statista.com/study/175921/second-trump-administration/).

## Who are the victims of violence?

Studies have shown that violent crime victims belong to a diverse range of [age groups](https://www.statista.com/statistics/424130/us-violent-crime-victims-by-age/) and are almost equally divided by [gender](https://www.statista.com/statistics/423245/us-violent-crime-victims-by-gender/). These patterns indicate that risk is driven less by demographic labels alone and more by underlying conditions such as poverty, insecure work, and limited chances for social mobility. For instance, [38 percent of violent crime victims come from households earning under 25,000 U.S. dollars](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1659485/violent-crime-victimiztion-rate-in-the-us-by-household-income/), compared with only 15.7 percent among households with incomes of 200,000 dollars or more.
